title: Ezekiel 33:1–9
context: The LORD’s word renews the watchman charge. First comes a general case: when the sword comes on a land, the people set a watchman, and if he blows the trumpet, anyone who does not heed it has “his blood” on “his own head” (33:2–5); if the watchman sees the sword and stays silent, the LORD will require the blood “at the watchman’s hand” (33:6). Then the LORD applies the case to the prophet: “I have set you a watchman to the house of Israel” (33:7–9). These verses closely repeat 3:17–19, where the charge stood at the prophet’s commissioning and also included cases of the righteous (3:20–21). Here it opens a new section of the book, after the oracles against the nations in chapters 25–32 and just before the news that the city has fallen (33:21). Each setting can be read in its own place. Both traditions affirm the prophet’s duty to warn, the hearer’s duty to turn, and the real accountability of each, as at 3:16–21.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to me, saying”. Arminian readers note that the watchman charge is renewed by the same word that first commissioned the prophet. The repetition marks a turning point, as the book moves toward the news of 33:21.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD himself renewing the prophet’s charge at a new stage in his ministry. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening formula as grounding what follows in the LORD’s authority rather than in the prophet’s own judgment.

verses.text: “Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and tell them, ‘When I bring the sword on a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and set him for their watchman,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sets out a case from ordinary life: when the sword comes on a land, the people “set him for their watchman”. Arminian readers note that the picture begins with a familiar civic duty, so that the hearers can grasp their own situation by analogy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a parable drawn from city defense, with the sword standing for judgment the LORD brings. Shared ground: both traditions read the watchman here as a public servant whose whole task is to see danger and warn, before the case is applied to the prophet in 33:7.

verses.text: if, when he sees the sword come on the land, he blows the trumpet and warns the people,
verses.arminianNotes: When the watchman “sees the sword come on the land, he blows the trumpet and warns the people”. Arminian readers note that the warning is given in time, while there is still opportunity to respond. Its purpose is that the people may escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the trumpet as a warning meant to be heeded, sounded before the danger arrives. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as defining the watchman’s faithfulness by the alarm he sounds, setting up the cases that follow.

verses.text: then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet and doesn’t heed the warning, if the sword comes and takes him away, his blood will be on his own head.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever hears and “doesn’t heed the warning” has “his blood” on “his own head.” Arminian readers note that the hearer who ignores a real warning bears his own guilt. The warning offered a genuine way of escape, and neglecting it is culpable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the hearer’s full responsibility for refusing a warning he has heard. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing the guilt where the refusal lies, with no blame left on the watchman who blew the trumpet.

verses.text: He heard the sound of the trumpet and didn’t take warning. His blood will be on him; whereas if he had heeded the warning, he would have delivered his soul.
verses.arminianNotes: “He heard the sound of the trumpet and didn’t take warning.” Arminian readers note the contrast with the one who heeds: “if he had heeded the warning, he would have delivered his soul.” The outcome turns on the response, and the response is real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the plain logic of the parable: the warned man who heeds is delivered, and the warned man who refuses is not. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that warnings are given for life, and that ignoring them is the hearer’s own fault.

verses.text: But if the watchman sees the sword come and doesn’t blow the trumpet, and the people aren’t warned, and the sword comes and takes any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman’s hand.’
verses.arminianNotes: If the watchman “doesn’t blow the trumpet,” the one taken is “taken away in his iniquity,” yet “his blood I will require at the watchman’s hand.” Arminian readers note that the silent watchman shares in the guilt, even though the one taken is not innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm two responsibilities at once: the person dies “in his iniquity,” and the watchman who kept silent is accountable to the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, as at 3:18, as joining the hearer’s guilt and the watchman’s duty without letting either cancel the other.

verses.text: “So you, son of man, I have set you a watchman to the house of Israel. Therefore hear the word from my mouth, and give them warnings from me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD applies the case: “I have set you a watchman to the house of Israel”, to “hear the word from my mouth, and give them warnings from me.” Arminian readers note that the warning is the LORD’s own. The prophet does not invent the danger he announces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophet appointed by the LORD to speak only what he hears from him. Shared ground: both traditions note that the verse closely repeats 3:17, while reading each in its own setting: there at the prophet’s commissioning, here as the book turns toward the city’s fall.

verses.text: When I tell the wicked, ‘O wicked man, you will surely die,’ and you don’t speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: When the LORD says, “O wicked man, you will surely die,” and the prophet does not warn, “that wicked man will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand.” Arminian readers note the weight of the prophet’s charge alongside the wicked man’s own guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm the wicked man’s real guilt and the prophet’s real accountability before the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, like 3:18, as a solemn charge to the messenger, not as a statement that the hearer is blameless when the warning is withheld.

verses.text: Nevertheless, if you warn the wicked of his way to turn from it, and he doesn’t turn from his way; he will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.
verses.arminianNotes: If the prophet warns the wicked “to turn from it,” and he does not turn, “he will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul.” Arminian readers note that the warning aims at a real turning, and that refusing it is the hearer’s own act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the faithful watchman cleared once he has warned, with the outcome resting on the hearer’s response under God’s governance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, like 3:19, as defining faithfulness by the warning given, not by the results achieved.
